snippets.title: Agentic Develop
snippets.text:
Not every repo is ready to run. Maybe it has no Dockerfile yet, or you just want an agent to work through it first. **Agentic Develop** brings the code into Rock8Cloud so agents can start on it, and deploys it the moment it can actually be built.

There is nothing to remember and nothing to switch on later. The rule is simply: **if the repo has a Dockerfile, it deploys. If it does not, it waits.**

***

snippets.title: Agentic Develop
snippets.heading: What Happens to Your Repo
snippets.text:
| Your repo        | What Rock8Cloud does                                               |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Has a Dockerfile | Creates the service and deploys it, same as always                 |
| No Dockerfile    | Creates the service and stops there. Nothing is built, no pods run |

A service waiting on a Dockerfile shows an empty **Deployments** tab. Nothing is built and no pods run for it, so it burns no build minutes. Its allocation does still count against your plan's resource pool from the moment it is created, so sleep, shrink or delete one you are no longer working on. See [Plans and usage](/docs/plans-and-usage).

<Callout type="info">
  **Blueprints always deploy in full.** A blueprint ships with working Dockerfiles, so picking one under Agentic Develop provisions everything that blueprint defines - its code, and whatever database or storage slots it comes with - exactly as **Deploy and Develop** would. Some are code only, such as Vue. You still get the agents, you just also get a running stack.
</Callout>

***

snippets.title: Agentic Develop
snippets.heading: Working on It
snippets.text:
Everything that needs only the repository works right away:

* **[Agents](/docs/guides/agents)** - coding and research sessions in a cloud sandbox. A coder session edits a checkout, pushes a branch and opens a pull request, exactly as it does on a deployed service.
* **Custom agents** and **agent workflows**
* **[Code reviews](/docs/guides/code-reviews)** on pull requests
* **Instructions** - the standing rules your agents follow on this service
* **[Environment variables](/docs/guides/environment-variables)** and build settings, so the first deploy is right when it comes

***

snippets.title: Notifications
snippets.heading: Setting Up Slack
snippets.text:
deployment starts, Rock8Cloud sends a "Deployment Started" message to your channel
2. When the deployment completes, the success or failure message is posted as a **reply in the same thread**
3. An emoji reaction is added to the original "Deployment Started" message:

   * :x: for failed deployments

snippets.title: Jira Integration
snippets.heading: Troubleshooting
snippets.text:
**The pairing link says it cannot be used.** Links last 15 minutes and work once. Go back to the Rock8Cloud page in Jira and click **Pair with Rock8Cloud** again. After 10 dead links or wrong codes, your whole organization waits up to 15 minutes before pairing accepts another attempt.

**The dialog says this Jira site is already connected.** The organization picked in the dialog already works with that site, so there is nothing to add and its projects are mappable under **Settings** → **Integrations** → **Jira** already. Pick a different organization in the same dialog, or cancel.

**Rock8Cloud says the project is already mapped, but it is not in my list.** Another organization on the same Jira site mapped that project. A project belongs to one organization. Your Jira site admin can see which organizations are connected on the Rock8Cloud page in Jira.

**Nothing happens when I assign the work item.** The project is not mapped, its mapping is **Paused**, or the mapped service has no repository attached. The Agents panel says which, and names the page that fixes it. Once it is fixed, reply "try again" in the panel and Rock8Cloud picks the work item back up, as long as you do it within a day. After that, assign the work item again. The Rock8Cloud page in Jira also lists the projects that are actually mapped.

**Rock8Cloud asks which repository every time.** The project is mapped to more than one and the work item's **Repository** field is empty. It is per work item, so a new ticket starts empty. Answering by reply saves it to the field, unless the field is missing from the project's screens - then the answer starts the run but cannot be stored, so the next work item asks again.

snippets.title: Bug Reports & Bounty
snippets.heading: Reporting a Bug
snippets.text:
1. Click **Bug bounty hunt** in the top bar
2. Choose **Report a bug**
3. Describe what you were trying to do and what happened
4. Optionally attach a screenshot (up to 5 MB)
5. Click **Submit**

The more specific the description, the faster it gets triaged. "Deploy button does nothing on the preview environment of service X" beats "deploys broken".

### What gets attached automatically [#what-gets-attached-automatically]

You do not need to collect diagnostics. Every report also carries:

* The page you were on and the full URL
* Browser, viewport size, and the app version you were running
* A snapshot of the data the app had loaded at that moment, as `debug-data.json`
* A session replay link, so the team can see the steps that led to it

This is why a one-line description is usually enough.

snippets.title: Next.js + React - Blueprint
snippets.heading: Project Structure
snippets.text:
```
app/
├── page.tsx                         # React client component: fetches API, renders table
├── layout.tsx                       # Root layout
└── api/
    ├── targets/route.ts             # GET /api/targets
    └── info/route.ts                # GET /api/info

lib/
├── db.ts                            # pg Pool (DATABASE_URL or DB_*), sslmode handling
└── migrate.ts                       # Reads and runs SQL files from db/migrations/

db/migrations/
└── V1__init.sql                     # Creates space_target table + seed data

instrumentation.ts                   # Next.js hook: runs migrations on server startup
next.config.ts                       # output: 'standalone' for Docker
```

**Key design decisions:**

* `app/page.tsx` is a `'use client'` component: it runs in the browser, calls `/api/info` and `/api/targets` via `fetch`, and renders the table once both requests succeed. The connection indicator dot reflects the fetch status.
* `lib/db.ts` strips `sslmode` from the connection string before passing it to `pg` because pg v8+ treats `sslmode=require` as `verify-full` (rejecting self-signed certs). SSL is instead controlled via the `ssl` object, with `rejectUnauthorized: false` for cloud-managed databases.
* Migrations run via Next.js `instrumentation.ts`, called once when the Node.js server starts.
* `next.config.ts` sets `output: 'standalone'` for minimal Docker images. The `db/` directory is copied separately in the Dockerfile because `instrumentation.ts` needs the migration files at runtime.
* To add a new endpoint: create a `route.ts` under `app/api/` and query via the pool from `lib/db.ts`. Update `app/page.tsx` to display the new data.

***

snippets.title: S3 Object Storage
snippets.heading: Troubleshooting
snippets.text:
### Access denied [#access-denied]

* Verify `S3_ACCESS_KEY` and `S3_SECRET_KEY` are correctly set
* Ensure the bucket name matches `S3_BUCKET`

### Connection issues [#connection-issues]

* Use the **internal endpoint** for service-to-service access within your project
* Use the **external URL** for access from outside your project
* Ensure `forcePathStyle: true` is set in your client configuration

### Region errors [#region-errors]

* The `S3_REGION` environment variable is set automatically - don't hardcode a region value
* If you see region-related errors, make sure `S3_REGION` is included in your service's environment variables

### Public URL returns `NoSuchKey` / 404 [#public-url-returns-nosuchkey--404]

The bucket was matched but the requested key isn't there. Almost always caused by uploading with path-style addressing - files end up under a `<bucket-name>/` prefix instead of at the root.

Check with `aws s3 ls s3://$S3_BUCKET/` (use virtual-hosted addressing, see [Uploading Files for Public Access](#uploading-files-for-public-access)). If you see your files under a folder matching the bucket name, re-upload after configuring `addressing_style = virtual`.

***

snippets.title: Next.js (API + Swagger) - Blueprint
snippets.heading: Project Structure
snippets.text:
```
app/
├── page.tsx                         # Redirects / → /swagger
├── swagger/
│   └── page.tsx                     # Swagger UI (client component, loads /api/openapi.json)
└── api/
    ├── targets/route.ts             # GET /api/targets
    ├── info/route.ts                # GET /api/info
    └── openapi.json/route.ts        # GET /api/openapi.json - serves the OpenAPI spec

lib/
├── db.ts                            # pg Pool (DATABASE_URL or DB_*)
└── migrate.ts                       # Reads and runs SQL files from db/migrations/

db/migrations/
└── V1__init.sql                     # Creates space_target table + seed data

instrumentation.ts                   # Next.js hook: runs migrations on server startup
next.config.ts                       # output: 'standalone' for Docker
```

**Key design decisions:**

* `lib/db.ts` creates a single `pg.Pool` that is reused across requests. It reads `DATABASE_URL` first and falls back to individual `DB_*` variables. SSL is enabled when `sslmode=require` appears in the URL or when `DB_SSL_MODE=require` is set.
* Migrations run via Next.js `instrumentation.ts`, which is called once when the Node.js server starts. This keeps migration logic out of request handlers.
* The OpenAPI spec in `app/api/openapi.json/route.ts` is hand-authored. The Swagger UI page loads it dynamically to avoid SSR issues with `swagger-ui-react`.
* `next.config.ts` sets `output: 'standalone'` so the Dockerfile can copy only the minimal runtime output (`/app/.next/standalone`). The `db/` directory is copied separately because `instrumentation.ts` needs the migration files at runtime after build.
* To add a new endpoint: create a `route.ts` under `app/api/`, query via the pool from `lib/db.ts`, and update the OpenAPI spec in `app/api/openapi.json/route.t

preview-expiry.query: Preview deployments disappear after a few days. I opened a preview URL from a PR I made last week and it 404s now. It worked when the PR was open.

snippets.title: Preview Deployments
snippets.heading: Cleanup
snippets.text:
Previews are automatically removed when the pull request is closed or merged. No manual cleanup needed.

### Deleting a preview manually [#deleting-a-preview-manually]

You can remove a preview before its pull request is closed, for example to free up capacity:

1. Select the preview environment (**PR #123** in the service sidebar)
2. Open the **Overview** tab
3. Open the actions menu in the header bar and choose **Delete environment**

The preview stops running and its URL goes away. The pull request itself is untouched, so pushing another commit to it creates the preview again.

snippets.title: Frequently Asked Questions
snippets.heading: Preview Deployments
snippets.text:
### What are preview deployments? [#what-are-preview-deployments]

Temporary deployments for pull requests. Each PR gets its own URL:

```
https://your-service-pr123.apps.rock8.cloud
```

Great for testing changes before merging!

### How do I enable preview deployments? [#how-do-i-enable-preview-deployments]

1. Go to your service's **Workflows** tab
2. Enable the **Preview Deployments** workflow (enabled by default)
3. Configure source branch patterns if needed (defaults to `feat/*`)

New PRs matching your branch patterns will automatically deploy.

### Do preview deployments use the same database? [#do-preview-deployments-use-the-same-database]

Yes, preview deployments use the same environment variables as your main deployment, including database connections.

If you need separation, create a separate project or service with its own database for preview/staging purposes.

### When are previews deleted? [#when-are-previews-deleted]

Automatically when you:

* Close the pull request
* Merge the pull request

No manual cleanup needed!

***

snippets.title: Preview Deployments
snippets.heading: How It Works
snippets.text:
1. You open a pull request on GitHub
2. Rock8Cloud builds and deploys a preview environment
3. A preview URL is available (e.g., `https://your-service-pr123.apps.rock8.cloud`)
4. Push more commits → the preview updates automatically
5. Close or merge the PR → the preview is cleaned up, or delete it yourself at any time

snippets.title: Preview Deployments
snippets.heading: Troubleshooting
snippets.text:
| Problem                                     | Solution                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No preview created                          | Check the workflow is enabled and branch patterns match       |
| Preview waiting for pod capacity            | It starts automatically when capacity is available            |
| Preview waiting because service is sleeping | Wake the service to resume the pending preview                |
| Preview not updating                        | Verify new commits triggered a `synchronize` event            |
| Preview not removed                         | Delete it manually from **Overview** → **Delete environment** |

env-not-inherited.query: Environment variables are not shared between services. I set DATABASE_URL on one service and another service in the same project cannot see it. Surely they should share?

snippets.title: Environment Variables
snippets.heading: Linked Variables
snippets.text:
Link environment variables from other services in your project - databases, S3 storage, or other application services. Linked variables are resolved securely at deploy time.

1. In the environment variables section, select a **source service** from the dropdown
2. Choose which **variable** to link (e.g., `HOST`, `PASSWORD`, `URL`)
3. Rock8Cloud injects the value automatically when your service deploys

Credentials like database passwords and S3 secret keys are stored as secrets and never exposed as plain text - they're injected directly into your running container at deploy time.

When you link a variable that depends on other variables (e.g., `URL` depends on `HOST`, `PORT`, `USER`, `PASSWORD`, `NAME`), the dependencies are automatically included.

snippets.title: PostgreSQL
snippets.heading: Environment Variables
snippets.text:
After creation, Rock8Cloud exposes these variables for your application to connect:

| Variable   | Description         | Example                                  |
| ---------- | ------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `HOST`     | Database hostname   | *(auto-generated)*                       |
| `PORT`     | Database port       | `5432`                                   |
| `NAME`     | Database name       | `postgres-main`                          |
| `USER`     | Username            | `app`                                    |
| `PASSWORD` | Password            | *(auto-generated)*                       |
| `URL`      | Full connection URL | `postgresql://app:pass@host:5432/dbname` |

### Linking to Your Application [#linking-to-your-application]

1. Go to your application service → **Deployments** → **Env Vars**
2. Add the database variables using the names expected by your framework

**Common framework patterns:**

```bash
# Node.js / Prisma / Drizzle
DATABASE_URL=<URL>

# Django
DATABASE_HOST=<HOST>
DATABASE_PORT=<PORT>
DATABASE_NAME=<NAME>
DATABASE_USER=<USER>
DATABASE_PASSWORD=<PASSWORD>

# Rails
DATABASE_URL=<URL>
```

After saving, your application automatically redeploys with the new configuration.

***

snippets.title: Environment Variables
snippets.heading: Preview Environments
snippets.text: Preview deployments use the **same environment variables** as your stable deployment. If you need isolation, create a separate project with its own database and credentials.

snippets.title: Next.js (API + Swagger) - Blueprint
snippets.heading: Environment Variables
snippets.text:
The application runs on port **3000** and requires a PostgreSQL database.

Database connection is configured via **one of two approaches**:

### Option A - Single connection URL (recommended for managed services) [#option-a---single-connection-url-recommended-for-managed-services]

| Variable       | Required | Example                                                 |
| -------------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DATABASE_URL` | yes      | `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/dbname?sslmode=require` |

### Option B - Individual variables [#option-b---individual-variables]

| Variable      | Required | Default     | Description                    |
| ------------- | -------- | ----------- | ------------------------------ |
| `DB_HOST`     | no       | `localhost` | Database host                  |
| `DB_PORT`     | no       | `5432`      | Database port                  |
| `DB_NAME`     | no       | `spacedb`   | Database name                  |
| `DB_USER`     | no       | `postgres`  | Database user                  |
| `DB_PASSWORD` | no       | `postgres`  | Database password              |
| `DB_SSL_MODE` | no       | *(none)*    | Set to `require` to enable SSL |

`DATABASE_URL` takes precedence. If it is set, the individual `DB_*` variables are ignored.

***

snippets.title: Strapi + Next.js - Blueprint
snippets.text: A content website built with [Strapi 5](https://strapi.io/) and [Next.js 16](https://nextjs.org/), managed as a [Turborepo](https://turborepo.dev/) monorepo. One repository, two services, a database, and a media bucket, all wired up on deploy. **Tech stack:** | Layer | Technology | | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | CMS | Strapi 5 (TypeScript), port 1337 | | Frontend | Next.js 16 App Router, Turbopack, standalone output, port 3000 | | Styling | Tailwind v4 + shadcn/ui | | Database | PostgreSQL via `DATABASE_URL` | | Media | S3-compatible object storage | Content model: a `Page` collection with dynamic-zone blocks, plus `Navbar` and `Footer` single types. View on GitHub → ***

snippets.title: S3 Object Storage
snippets.heading: Deleting an S3 Service
snippets.text:
1. Go to your project
2. Select the S3 service
3. Click **Delete**
4. Confirm the deletion

Deleting an S3 service removes the storage and all stored data permanently.

***

snippets.title: Preview Deployments
snippets.heading: Cleanup
snippets.text:
Previews are automatically removed when the pull request is closed or merged. No manual cleanup needed.

### Deleting a preview manually [#deleting-a-preview-manually]

You can remove a preview before its pull request is closed, for example to free up capacity:

1. Select the preview environment (**PR #123** in the service sidebar)
2. Open the **Overview** tab
3. Open the actions menu in the header bar and choose **Delete environment**

The preview stops running and its URL goes away. The pull request itself is untouched, so pushing another commit to it creates the preview again.

snippets.title: Preview Deployments
snippets.heading: Troubleshooting
snippets.text:
| Problem                                     | Solution                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| No preview created                          | Check the workflow is enabled and branch patterns match       |
| Preview waiting for pod capacity            | It starts automatically when capacity is available            |
| Preview waiting because service is sleeping | Wake the service to resume the pending preview                |
| Preview not updating                        | Verify new commits triggered a `synchronize` event            |
| Preview not removed                         | Delete it manually from **Overview** → **Delete environment** |

snippets.title: Teams and Organizations
snippets.heading: Delete an Organization
snippets.text:
Only **owners** can delete an organization.

1. Go to **Settings** → **Organization**
2. Click **Delete Organization**
3. Confirm the deletion

This removes all projects, services, and associated resources permanently.
